gaps: Primary source is the LLBC 'British Columbia Executive Council Appointments (1871-1986)' (Oath Book / BC Gazette dates); Wikipedia ministry articles were cross-checked and disagree in several places (noted per record). LLBC preferred.

Vacancies: Minister of Public Works and Minister of Railways 1942-08-30 to 1942-09-04 (Bruhn's death); Lands and Municipal Affairs 1944-05-07 to 1944-05-11 (Gray's death); Agriculture 1945-11-19 to 1945-11-21; Attorney-General 1946-03-28 to 1946-04-04; Education 1953-10-12 to 1953-10-19 (Rolston's death); Agriculture 1957-04-03 to 1957-04-10 (Chetwynd's death).
Acting ministers during Wells Gray's illness before May 1944 (Hart for Lands, Anscomb for Municipal Affairs per Wikipedia) have no dates in the sources; not recorded.
Hart's 1942 and 1944 stints and Bennett's 1957 Agriculture and 1968 Highways stints are Oath Book appointments, recorded as acting=false even though they were stop-gaps.

Excluded per brief: ministers without portfolio (Buda Brown 1960-62; Isabel Dawson, Patricia Jordan, Grace McCarthy 1966-72; Gaglardi 1968-69; Frank Calder 1972-73; Lorne Nicolson and Phyllis Young 1973, responsible for housing and consumer services; Alf Nunweiler 1974-75) and Eileen Dailly's Deputy Premier designation (from 1972-09-26).

Party labels: Hart-era Conservatives are labelled 'Conservative' (the party became Progressive Conservative in 1942); Johnson-era ones 'Progressive Conservative', following the Wikipedia tables. The LLBC source gives no per-minister party.

Portfolio titles follow LLBC's Constitution Act styling ('Attorney-General', 'Minister of Lands, Forests, and Water Resources'); formal 'Minister of' wording before the short names is assumed from the source's convention of listing short names.
